title: Ehud at Gilgal: “quarries” or carved images?
summary: The KJV says Ehud turned back from “the quarries” by Gilgal. The Hebrew word is the plural the KJV elsewhere renders “graven images”, and the Septuagint has “the carved things”.
text: KJV Judges 3:19: “turned again from the quarries that were by Gilgal”; 3:26: “passed beyond the quarries”. Hebrew (WLC): 3:19 מִן־הַפְּסִילִים֙ אֲשֶׁ֣ר אֶת־הַגִּלְגָּ֔ל [from the carved images that are by Gilgal]; 3:26 עָבַ֣ר אֶת־הַפְּסִילִ֔ים. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): 3:19 ἀπὸ τῶν γλυπτῶν τῶν μετὰ τῆς Γαλγάλ [from the carved things by Galgal]; 3:26 παρῆλθε τὰ γλυπτὰ. The same Hebrew plural at Deuteronomy 7:25, פְּסִילֵ֥י אֱלֹהֵיהֶ֖ם, is “The graven images of their gods” in the KJV. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/3/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG03.htm and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/5/7/.
reasoning: Hebrew and Greek agree against the KJV. On their wording, carved images stood near Gilgal, Israel’s first camp in the land, in the time of the judges; the KJV’s “quarries” removes that.
scope: The verses do not say whose images these were or who made them, so no violation is claimed. A shared Hebrew word does not prove the same kind of object in both books. Brenton’s own English translation prints “quarries” beside this Greek. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier. title: Israel served “the groves”: trees, or Asherah?
summary: The KJV says Israel served “Baalim and the groves”. The Hebrew has “the Asheroth”, the plural of Asherah; “groves” is the Septuagint’s word. Elsewhere the KJV’s “grove” has prophets and is carried out of the temple.
text: KJV Judges 3:7: “served Baalim and the groves”. Hebrew (WLC): וַיַּעַבְד֥וּ אֶת־הַבְּעָלִ֖ים וְאֶת־הָאֲשֵׁרֹֽות [and they served the Baals and the Asheroth]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): ἐλάτρευσαν τοῖς Βααλὶμ καὶ τοῖς ἄλσεσι [they served the Baalim and the groves]. Judges 6:25 (KJV): “cut down the grove that is by it”; Hebrew וְאֶת־הָאֲשֵׁרָ֥ה. 1 Kings 18:19 (KJV): “the prophets of the groves four hundred”; Hebrew וּנְבִיאֵ֤י הָֽאֲשֵׁרָה֙ [and the prophets of the Asherah]. 2 Kings 23:6 (KJV): “he brought out the grove from the house of the Lord” … “and burned it”; Hebrew וַיֹּצֵ֣א אֶת־הָאֲשֵׁרָה֩ מִבֵּ֨ית יְהוָ֜ה. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/3/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG03.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/6/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/11/18/ and https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/12/23/.
reasoning: The KJV follows the Greek sense, a stand of trees, where the Hebrew has a name-like word paired with the Baals as something served. The KJV’s own usage shows the strain: its “grove” has four hundred prophets and is carried out of a building and burned.
scope: This record does not decide whether the word names a goddess, a wooden object or both; that needs a lexicon and outside sources not opened here. It shows only that “groves” is the Greek translators’ word, not a rendering of the Hebrew word’s form. The same rendering runs through the KJV Old Testament and is not listed verse by verse. title: Left-handed, or able to use both hands?
summary: The KJV calls Ehud and seven hundred Benjamite slingers “lefthanded”. The Hebrew says, word for word, “bound in his right hand”. The Septuagint says “ambidextrous”.
text: KJV Judges 3:15: “a Benjamite, a man lefthanded”; 20:16: “seven hundred chosen men lefthanded”. Hebrew (WLC), both verses: אִ֥ישׁ אִטֵּ֖ר יַד־יְמִינֹ֑ו [a man bound, or restricted, in his right hand]; אִטֵּ֖ר יַד־יְמִינֹ֑ו. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): 3:15 ἄνδρα ἀμφοτεροδέξιον [a man with two right hands, ambidextrous]; 20:16 ἀμφοτεροδέξιοι. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/3/, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/20/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG03.htm and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG20.htm.
reasoning: The Greek gives the men full use of both hands; the Hebrew phrase speaks of a limit on the right hand; the KJV says left-handed. The Greek and the KJV describe different abilities.
scope: The KJV’s “lefthanded” is a fair rendering of the Hebrew idiom, so no H tag is proposed; the difference tagged is between the Greek and the KJV. Whether the Hebrew phrase means a disability, a trained habit or plain left-handedness is not settled by its wording. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier. title: Past oppressors: Maonites or Midian?
summary: In God’s list of peoples he saved Israel from, the KJV and the Hebrew name Maon; the Septuagint names Midian.
text: KJV Judges 10:12: “The Zidonians also, and the Amalekites, and the Maonites, did oppress you”. Hebrew (WLC): וְצִידֹונִ֤ים וַֽעֲמָלֵק֙ וּמָעֹ֔ון [and Sidonians and Amalek and Maon]. Septuagint (Brenton Greek): καὶ Σιδωνίων, καὶ Ἀμαλὲκ, καὶ Μαδιὰμ [and Sidonians and Amalek and Madiam, Midian]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/10/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG10.htm.
reasoning: The two traditions name different peoples in the same list. Judges 6–8 narrates a Midianite oppression and deliverance, which the Greek reading would recall.
scope: That no Maonite oppression is narrated earlier is an observation about what the book tells, not proof that none was meant. Do not claim either reading is original. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. title: Sisera’s death in narrative and song
summary: The narrative kills Sisera while he sleeps; the song describes him falling at Jael’s feet. KJV says she struck off his head, while ASV and WEB say she struck through it. A literal sequence needs qualification.
text: Judges 4:21-22 describes Jael driving a tent peg through a sleeping Sisera and into the ground; Barak sees the peg in his temples. Judges 5:26-27 poetically repeats his bowing, falling and lying at her feet. The packaged KJV says she smote off his head; the packaged ASV and WEB instead describe striking through his head. Original-language wording of 5:26: the KJV has “she smote off his head”. The Hebrew (WLC) has מָחֲקָ֣ה רֹאשֹׁ֔ו [she struck, or crushed, his head], with no word for “off”. The Brenton Greek has διήλωσε κεφαλὴν αὐτοῦ [she nailed through his head]. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/5/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG05.htm.
reasoning: Treating the song as a precise standing-to-falling chronology creates tension with a sleeper pinned to the ground. Poetic repetition can describe death without specifying an earlier standing posture. The KJV head wording suggests a different action, but the translations show that this stronger contrast is edition-dependent; the narrative also does not explicitly deny any additional blow.
scope: Do not assert all translations describe decapitation, that the man must have been standing, or that the two texts prove two deaths. Literary posture and translation choices require interpretation. This is not independent forensic or historical evidence. The poem’s stars and melting mountains are not automatically literal science claims. Neither the Hebrew nor the Greek edition quoted describes a head being removed, so the decapitation contrast belongs to the KJV’s wording. The exact sense of the Hebrew verb is the researcher’s gloss, not a lexicon ruling. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier.

title: Moses’ relatives and the in-law label
summary: KJV calls Hobab Moses’ father-in-law; ASV and WEB call him brother-in-law. Exodus names Reuel and Jethro, while Numbers calls Hobab Reuel’s son. The apparent family conflict depends on the kinship reading.
text: Exodus 2:18 names the daughters’ father Reuel, and 2:21 gives Zipporah to Moses. Exodus 3:1 calls Jethro Moses’ father-in-law and priest of Midian. Numbers 10:29 introduces Hobab son of Raguel the Midianite, followed by the in-law label. Judges 4:11 calls Hobab father-in-law in the packaged KJV but brother-in-law in the packaged ASV and WEB. Judges 1:16 associates Moses’ in-law family with the Kenites. Original-language wording: at Judges 1:16 the KJV has “the children of the Kenite, Moses' father in law” and the Hebrew (WLC) likewise gives no personal name: וּבְנֵ֣י קֵינִי֩ חֹתֵ֨ן מֹשֶׁ֜ה. The Brenton Greek supplies one: οἱ υἱοὶ Ἰοθὸρ τοῦ Κιναίου τοῦ γαμβροῦ Μωυσῆ [the sons of Jothor, Jethro, the Kenite, Moses’ in-law]. At Judges 4:11 the Hebrew has חֹבָ֖ב חֹתֵ֣ן מֹשֶׁ֑ה and the Greek Ἰωβὰβ γαμβροῦ Μωυσῆ. Fetched from https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/1/, https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG01.htm, https://bolls.life/get-text/WLC/7/4/ and https://ebible.org/grcbrent/JDG04.htm.
reasoning: If every in-law label denotes the same paternal relationship, the named father and son create tension. Reading Hobab as brother-in-law avoids that particular generation conflict; equating Jethro and Reuel as two names for one person is a possible explanation, not an explicit identification in these passages. Numbers’ punctuation alone does not prove which antecedent receives the label.
scope: This comparison is edition-sensitive. Do not claim all translations make Hobab the father-in-law, or that Kenite and Midianite must be mutually exclusive ethnic identities. No original-language semantic range or family genealogy is established solely from English translations. Alias and clan relationships remain interpretation questions. The Greek of Judges 1:16 names Jethro where the Hebrew and KJV name no one, so in the Greek book both Jethro (1:16) and Hobab (4:11) carry the same in-law word. Brenton’s English renders that Greek word “father-in-law” in both verses; the same Greek word is used for the woman’s father at Judges 19:9, so it does not by itself fix the relationship. The Hebrew quoted is the Westminster Leningrad Codex digital text and the Greek is Brenton’s printed edition of the Septuagint, an ancient translation tradition. A digital named edition is not proof that every manuscript agrees, and neither edition settles which reading is earlier.
